A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SAFESEARCH study and provide readable main text, figures, tables, and Appendices A–M. Existing material can be matched reliably across the additions, moves, and renumbering.

before.justification: V4 reports original search-agent evaluations in Table 1, two in-the-wild investigations, configuration ablations, and human validation of its safety evaluator.

after.justification: V5 retains those original empirical results and adds controlled scaffold comparisons, robustness evaluations, and a non-injected-response analysis.

M1.justification: The test-generation workflow, differential filtering, single-website injection procedure, and default evaluation method remain unchanged, as do the Appendix M prompts. Alternative generators, judges, and forced-search variants are evaluated as experimental comparisons rather than adopted as changes to SAFESEARCH.

E1.justification: V5 adds evaluation with Jina and Tavily search backends alongside Google in Table 14, extending the retrieval environments tested. Jina previously served as a webpage reader. The 300-case benchmark, five risk categories, and auxiliary query datasets remain unchanged.

E2.justification: V5 adds forced variants to the scaffold comparison in Table 2; forced tool-calling previously appeared only in the injection-round ablation. It also evaluates Gemini-2.5-Flash as an alternative website generator and adds safety-judge comparisons involving DeepSeek-V3.1, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Gemini-3-Flash, Qwen3-32B, and a five-judge majority. The main agent and defense comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: Table 2 introduces an important controlled design: automatic and forced tool-calling/deep-research variants are compared at search budgets of 3, 6, and 9. Additional protocols include evaluating the same 500 responses with multiple judges and testing alternative generators and search backends. These extend the evaluation design; the original benchmark settings are not reported as changed.

E4.justification: V5 substantially expands validation by testing whether scaffold advantages survive matched search budgets and whether results depend on generator family, safety judge, or search backend. Appendix I also adds manual analysis of eight flagged non-injected responses. The existing injection-position, token-limit, timestamp, persuasiveness, and test-generator analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report three trials per test case and averaged ASR/HS. V5 introduces no confidence intervals, significance tests, seed disclosures, or increased repetition counts. The cross-judge comparison reports robustness to evaluator choice rather than a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the matched existing appendix results are unchanged, but v5 adds consequential findings. At nine forced searches, Table 2 reports 36.67% ASR for tool-calling versus 46.16% for deep research, qualifying the original default-setting ranking. New results also cover generator/backend robustness, judge ASRs of 45.0–47.6%, and eight flagged responses among 900 non-injected trials. These are additional results, not replacements for the original scores.

T1.justification: The threat-model assumptions and mathematical description of injected search results in Section 3 are retained. V5 adds empirical controls and explanatory discussion, without new formal definitions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

C1.justification: The framework contribution, benchmark scope, and central vulnerability claim remain. The introduction narrows the scaffold-related finding from generally stronger resilience with deep research to stronger resilience through effective search-budget use. The explicit three-part contribution summary largely restates existing contributions.

C2.justification: V5 materially revises the explanation of scaffold differences: Section 4.2 attributes much of the autonomous deep-research advantage to fuller budget use and rejects unconditional scaffold superiority. Section 5 explicitly limits simulated ASR to controlled susceptibility rather than deployed failure prevalence. Appendices G, I, and J add interpretations of judge/backend robustness and acknowledge that the non-injected sanity check does not provide full real-world calibration.

D1.justification: Appendix J.3 newly quantifies reproduction cost: $8.53 for a Gemini-2.5-Flash tool-calling evaluation on 300 cases, including $6.41 for reusable test cases and websites, excluding search costs. Existing implementation descriptions, prompts, and code/data access information remain. Some new experiments still lack precise model-version and execution-setting details.

R1.justification: Related-work positioning is essentially retained, but Appendix J.1 removes the Google Search safety-page citation accompanying its earlier search-service limitation. Bibliographic changes to DeepSeek-R1, WideSearch, and Who Taught the Lie update retained works to publication records rather than adding new research.

P1.justification: V5 makes localized introduction and discussion rewrites, adds an explicit contribution summary and acknowledgements, replaces 'harmless' with 'sandboxed,' and updates the publication imprint. The main section sequence and Appendix A–M organization remain intact.

P2.justification: V5 adds four compact tables—Tables 2, 8, 11, and 14—and reflows surrounding material and renumbers retained tables. Existing figure artwork is unchanged. Several appendix captions receive typo or model-name corrections; there is no broad visual redesign.

improvement.justification: The matched-budget comparison makes the scaffold conclusions more defensible, while additional robustness checks, explicit limits on simulated ASR, and cost disclosure strengthen an already extensive empirical study. The overall gain is bounded: the new controls cover limited agent configurations, some new settings are incompletely documented, and similar aggregate judge ASRs do not establish case-level agreement. The core benchmark evidence remains unchanged.
